summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for the Link Layer protocol of X.25, called LAPB. It lets management software monitor those links.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of gauges for the first layer of an X.25 connection, so you can see how well that line is doing.

questions: what is the x.25 lapb mib
what tables does the lapb mib define
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching and configuring the LAPB link layer that sits under X.25.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a standard way to inspect and configure the LAPB link layer of an X.25 stack from an SNMP management station.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB module defines four tables under lapb (transmission 16): lapbAdmnTable for configured values, lapbOperTable for values in use, lapbFlowTable for traffic and state statistics, and lapbXidTable for XID frame fields.
tldr.outcome: Together with the X.25 packet layer MIB and the RS-232-like MIB it lets all three layers of an X.25 stack be managed. The RFC says security issues are not discussed.

today: RFC 1381 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1992, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Network Management Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for TCP/IP-based internets, specifically objects for managing LAPB, the Link Layer of X.25. The Internet-standard framework has three components: rules for defining objects (the SMI, RFC 1155, with concise definitions in RFC 1212), the object definitions themselves (MIB-II is in RFC 1213), and the protocol for manipulating them (SNMP, RFC 1157).

The MIB is an abstract tree. Branches name objects and leaves hold the values that management reads and writes. Objects are named with ASN.1 object identifiers, and each also has a textual object descriptor for human convenience.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a big filing cabinet where every drawer has a label. A manager can look up any label and read or change what is inside.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
A system with a complete X.25 stack over a synchronous line has at least two interfaces in the MIB-II ifTable: one for LAPB and one for the X.25 packet layer. The RS-232-like MIB covers the physical sync line. Each layer identifies the one below it: the X.25 object x25InfoDataLinkId names an instance of lapbAdmnIndex, and lapbOperPortId names the sync line LAPB uses.

A system with two X.25 lines would have two ifTable entries for the packet layers and two for the LAPB interfaces. LAPB interfaces are identified by an ifType of lapb(16), and the relationship between a LAPB interface and an ifTable interface is one-to-one, so ifIndex directly selects the matching entries in this MIB.

The definitions follow ISO 7776 and ISO 8885, and use the term DCE/remote DTE for the peer. The MIB may be applied to a LAPB acting as either a DCE or a DTE. Two textual conventions, PositiveInteger and IfIndexType, are introduced only for readability and change no syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: An X.25 connection is like a stack of pancakes, and each pancake has its own set of gauges. This document covers the gauges for the pancake that handles the link.

sections.title: The Four Tables
sections.content:
The extension adds four tables:

  • lapbAdmnTable: common parameters such as the T1 retransmission timer and N2 retransmission counter. The values are read-write and give the values used to initialize an interface.
  • lapbOperTable: the parameters actually in use, read only. They may differ from the Admn values if the Admn table changed after startup or XID negotiation chose other values.
  • lapbFlowTable: read-only objects that report how the interface performs.
  • lapbXidTable: the XID frame fields not already in the Admn table, read-write. It is only for systems that use XID negotiation.

Support for the Admn, Oper and Flow tables is mandatory for agents of systems that implement LAPB. The DEFVAL clauses give reasonable but not mandatory defaults and do not imply a way to create or delete LAPB interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one sheet for what you asked for, one for what is really happening, one for the counters, and one for special negotiation settings.

sections.title: Configured and Operating Parameters
sections.content:
The Admn and Oper tables cover station type (dte, dce or dxe), control field size (modulo8 or modulo128), maximum frame sizes in bits (N1), window sizes (K, from 1 to 127), the N2 retry count and four timers. Window size is the maximum number of unacknowledged sequenced PDUs outstanding.

Defaults in the Admn table include station type dte, modulo8, an N1 of 36000 bits (4500 * 8), K of 7, N2 of 20, a T1 acknowledgement timer of 3000 milliseconds, a T2 acknowledgement delay of 0 (no delay), a T3 disconnect timer of 60000 milliseconds, and a T4 idle timer of 2147483647 (no idle timer). Two further Admn objects, lapbAdmnActionInitiate and lapbAdmnActionRecvDM, choose how link setup is started and what to do on receiving a DM.

The Oper table also reports lapbOperPortId, the object identifying the physical device in use (or {0 0} if the agent supports none), and lapbOperProtocolVersionId.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the settings of the line, like how many messages can be on the way at once and how long to wait for a reply before trying again.

sections.title: Flow Statistics and Traps
sections.content:
The Flow table gives a window into how the link behaves. Objects include lapbFlowStateChanges (a count of state changes including resets), lapbFlowChangeReason, lapbFlowCurrentMode, lapbFlowBusyDefers, lapbFlowRejOutPkts, lapbFlowRejInPkts, lapbFlowT1Timeouts and the last FRMR frames sent and received.

The current mode takes values such as disconnected, linkSetup, frameReject, disconnectRequest, informationTransfer, rejFrameSent, waitingAcknowledgement and stationBusy.

Because every LAPB interface has an ifTable entry, significant state changes should send a linkUp or linkDown trap. An interface that sends or receives a Frame Reject frame should send a linkDown trap, and a linkUp trap if it later recovers.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters tell you how often the line stumbled and why. If something goes badly wrong, the line can send out an alarm.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Note that the Admn and Xid tables are read-write, so how access to them is controlled is left to the management framework in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not say how to keep the dials safe from people who should not touch them.
